chunks: Serpentining a differential pair. The question: What is serpentining? Why is it important for diff pairs?
Serpentining a differential pair means adding a small zig-zag of extra length to the shorter trace so both traces arrive at the same time.
You add it right where the difference appears, such as just after a bend. If the whole pair needs to be longer, you meander both traces together so they stay equal.
Imagine two people walking side by side around a curve. The person on the outside walks farther. To arrive together, the inside person takes a small detour right after the curve.
If they waited until the end, they would have been out of step the whole way. And the detour must stay close, so they remain a pair.
(A) after a bend the outer (black) trace is longer, so a small jog on the inner (orange) trace restores equality. (B) To lengthen both traces equally, meander the pair as a pair.
(C) Avoid: a long detour of one trace pulls it away from its partner, raises the differential impedance and creates a fresh asymmetry.
Intra-pair skew: the arrival-time difference between the two traces of one pair ("Differential pair skew: why it matters, how to fix").
Jog: a small zig-zag added to the shorter trace to give it extra length. Pitch: the center-to-center distance between the two traces, equal to width plus gap.
Coupled meander: a serpentine in which the whole pair winds together, so both traces gain equal length.
Speed-up: tight legs couple, so a meander adds less delay than its length suggests ("Serpentining for bus synchronization").
Take 0. 24 mm traces with a 0. 2 mm gap, so the pitch is 0. 44 mm. A 90 degree bend makes the outer trace longer by 0. 44 times pi over 2 about 0. 69 mm. At 5.
9 picoseconds per millimeter, that is about 4. 1 picoseconds of skew. A U-shaped jog of height H adds about 2 henries of length, so H about 0. 345 mm on the inner trace fixes it.
"Serpentining a pair means adding a small jog or accordion to the shorter trace so both halves have equal delay.
It matters because intra-pair skew converts differential signal to common-mode: that closes the eye and causes EMI. A 90 degree bend can leave about 0.

7 mm, around 4 picoseconds, of imbalance, so I add compensation right after the bend, with 45 degree corners, legs spaced several trace widths apart, and without pulling the trace far from its partner.
To lengthen a whole pair I meander both traces together."
